The exact title match is **PMID 25084611**, “Dosimetric Inhomogeneity Predicts for Long-Term Breast Pain After Breast-Conserving Therapy.” It reports a cross-sectional questionnaire study of 355 eligible patients treated in 2007–2011; 285 responded (80%), and 135/285 (47%) reported pain in the treated breast.

Higher breast volume receiving **≥110%** of the prescribed dose independently predicted pain (OR **1.01 per cc**, 95% CI **1.003–1.017**, **P=.007**). Volume receiving ≥105% was associated only in univariable analysis (OR 1.001 per cc, 95% CI 1.000–1.002, P=.045). The abstract does **not** give a specific follow-up duration; it reports that shorter time since treatment also predicted pain (OR 0.98 per month, P=.03). This is a positive association, not a negative finding, and does not establish causality.

Yes. In the study titled “Dosimetric Inhomogeneity Predicts for Long-Term Breast Pain After Breast-Conserving Therapy” (PMID: 25084611), 135 of 285 questionnaire respondents reported pain in the treated breast. A larger breast volume receiving at least 110% of the prescribed dose independently predicted pain (OR 1.01 per cc; 95% CI 1.003–1.017; P=.007). The volume receiving at least 105% was associated with pain only in univariable analysis.

This was a cross-sectional observational study, so it shows an association rather than proving that dose inhomogeneity causes pain. The abstract did not specify an exact follow-up duration. Sources: `call_xqNTXddPL3ODXjh46LR0ZP4t`, `call_eDj7eIwyAHSjTHxx6VGmReZN`.

FINAL DECISION: YES
